title: Practical 1: Version control with Git and GitHub
text:
First repository in Git Bash
We first learn the commands in the command line. This way you will understand what happens in the background when you later click buttons in RStudio.

Create a repository on GitHub

On GitHub click + (top right) → New repository.
Fill in:

Repository name: e.g. git-practice
Visibility: Private or Public
tick Add a README file. The README is the “home page” of the repository with a short description of the project.

Click Create repository.




The new repository form: name, visibility (Private) and README.




git clone: download the repository to your computer
On the repository page click the green Code button and copy the HTTPS address. Other options are also available:







Option
When to use it




HTTPS
cloning with git clone (Git Bash, RStudio)


Open with GitHub Desktop
if you prefer a graphical program


Download ZIP
a one-off download without the Git history. Do not use it for the practicals.






The Code button on the repository page. Copy the HTTPS address with the icon to the right of the link.


In Git Bash, move to the folder where you want to keep your projects and clone the repository:
mkdir -p ~/GitHub
cd ~/GitHub
git clone https://github.com/USERNAME/git-practice.git
Cloning into 'git-practice'...
remote: Enumerating objects: 3, done.
remote: Counting objects: 100% (3/3), done.
remote: Total 3 (delta 0), reused 0 (delta 0), pack-reused 0
Receiving objects: 100% (3/3), done.
Move into the new repository folder:
cd git-practice
Git Bash shows some useful information in the command line: the user name and computer in green, the current folder in yellow and, when you are inside a Git repository, the current branch in blue (e.g. (main)).



The Git Bash prompt: user and computer (green), MINGW64 (purple), folder (yellow) and branch (blue).


The (main) label appears only when you are inside a Git repository folder. If you move out (cd ..), it disappears. This way you always see whether you are in the right place.
Look at what is in the folder. The ls -a command also lists hidden files and folders (those starting with a dot):
ls -a
./  ../  .git/  README.md
You created README.md on GitHub. .git/ is a hidden folder where Git stores the entire history of the project: all commits, branches and the link to GitHub. This folder is what turns an ordinary folder into a Git repository. If you delete it, the files stay, but the history is lost and the (main) label disappears. Never edit the .git folder by hand.






NasvetHidden folders in Explorer and Finder



The .git folder is hidden. On Windows you see it in File Explorer via View → Show → Hidden items; on macOS in Finder with Cmd + Shift + period.




git status: what has changed?
git status is the command you will use most often. It shows the state of the working directory compared to the last commit.
git status
On branch main
Your branch is up to date with 'origin/main'.

nothing to commit, working tree clean
Add a new file to the folder, e.g. scripts/test.R (create a scripts folder and an empty file in it). Run git status again:
On branch main
Your branch is up to date with 'origin/main'.

Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
        scripts/

nothing added to commit but untracked files present (use "git add" to track)
New files that Git does not track yet (untracked) are shown in red.



Files that Git does not track yet are shown in red.




git add: stage changes
git add scripts/test.R   # one file
git add .                # all changes in the current folder (careful!)
Check again with git status. Files ready to be committed are shown in green:
Changes to be committed:
  (use "git restore --staged <file>..." to unstage)
        new file:   scripts/test.R



After git add the file is shown in green and is ready to be committed.




git commit: save a snapshot
git commit -m "Add test script"
[main 0c879b4] Add test script
 1 file changed, 0 insertions(+), 0 deletions(-)
 create mode 100644 scripts/test.R
Every commit gets a unique identifier (hash, here 0c879b4) that you can later use to return to it.






NasvetA good commit message



The message should briefly say what you changed, e.g. Add SNP filtering by MAF or Fix y axis on PCA plot. Avoid messages such as fixes, asdf or new version. A month later they will tell you nothing.



Shortcut: git commit -a
git commit -a -m "Update existing scripts"
This command stages and commits changes to already tracked files in one step. It does not add new (untracked) files. Until you get used to Git, prefer the separate git add and git commit steps.



git push: send changes to GitHub
git push
To https://github.com/USERNAME/git-practice.git
   c82b3ae..0c879b4  main -> main
Refresh the repository page on GitHub. The new file and the commit are now visible there too.



The repository on GitHub after push: the new folder and the commit message.




git pull: bring changes from GitHub
On GitHub, edit the README.md file in the browser (pencil icon → Commit changes). This simulates a change made by someone else, or by you on another computer. Then, on your computer:
git pull
Updating 0c879b4..5e1a2f3
Fast-forward
 README.md | 2 ++
 1 file changed, 2 insertions(+)
If there is nothing new on GitHub, Git prints Already up to date.






OpozoriloGood habit



At the start of every work session, run git pull first and only then start editing files. This way you avoid conflicts.




git log and git diff: history and differences
git log --oneline     # short list of all commits
git diff              # what you changed but have not added with git add yet
git diff --staged     # what is staged for the next commit
5e1a2f3 (HEAD -> main, origin/main) Update README.md
0c879b4 Add test script
c82b3ae Initial commit


git init: a new repository from an existing folder
If the project already exists on your computer and you want to put it under version control now:
cd path/to/project
git init
Initialized empty Git repository in .../project/.git/
Git creates a hidden .git folder where it keeps the entire history (HEAD, objects, refs …). Do not edit or delete this folder, as that deletes the whole history.
To connect the local repository to GitHub, create an empty repository on GitHub (without a README) and then:
git remote add origin https://github.com/USERNAME/project.git
git push -u origin main






Opombaclone or init?




git clone: a copy of an existing repository from GitHub. This is the most common way and the one we use in the practicals.
git init: a new local repository that you connect to GitHub later.

Created by

yes

yes

RStudio
yes

GitHub rejects files larger than 100 MB. The eagle VCF file we will work with is almost 600 MB.
The data do not change during the analysis and are already stored elsewhere (e.g. in the Dryad repository that accompanies the paper). GitHub is for the code that turns data into results.

text:
When something goes wrong: undoing changes







Situation
Command




I changed a file and want the last saved version back
git restore file.R


I added a file with git add but do not want it in the commit
git restore --staged file.R


The last commit has a wrong message (not pushed yet)
git commit --amend -m "New message"


I want to undo a commit that is already on GitHub
git revert <hash> (creates a new commit that reverses the changes)









Opozorilo



git restore file.R permanently discards unsaved changes in the file. Check with git diff before using it.



When two people work at the same time
What happens when two people (Ana and Bor) work on the same repository and both send their changes to GitHub?



Ana and Bor work at the same time. Bor pushes first. GitHub rejects Ana’s push because it has commit C, which Ana does not have yet. Ana therefore runs git pull first (combining Bor’s commit with hers) and only then pushes successfully.


Why this is good:

nobody can accidentally overwrite someone else’s work: Git rejects the push until you have all changes from GitHub,
both people’s work is kept: after git pull the history contains both commits, C and D,
Git does most of the merging itself; it only needs your help with a conflict.

The same happens when you work alone on two computers (e.g. at home and at the faculty). Hence the rule: always git pull before you start working.


Conflicts
A conflict happens when the same line of the same file was changed in two places (e.g. on GitHub and on your computer). On pull, Git writes markers into the file:
<<<<<<< HEAD
plot(pca$x[, 1], pca$x[, 2], col = "blue")
=======
plot(pca$x[, 1], pca$x[, 2], col = "red")
>>>>>>> origin/main
The upper part is your version, the lower part is the version from GitHub. Manually keep the correct line, delete the <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>> markers, and then git add, git commit and git push.
When working in your own repository from one computer, you avoid conflicts by consistently following the pull → work → commit → push loop.

text:
Branches
Branches let you develop new things or try out ideas without breaking the working main version (main). In the practicals you will mostly work on main, but branches are the basis of every team project.

main should stay as stable as possible,
each person or each new feature gets its own branch,
when the work is finished and tested, the branch is merged back into main.




Branch test splits off main, we make two commits on it and then merge it back into main with git merge.



Creating and switching branches
git branch                 # list local branches (* = current)
git switch -c new-plot     # create a new branch and switch to it
git switch main            # go back to main
git branch -d new-plot     # delete the branch (once it is merged)






Opombagit switch or git checkout?



In older tutorials and figures you will often see git checkout (git checkout -b new-branch). The command works, but it does two different jobs: switching branches and restoring files, which confuses beginners. Newer Git commands split them: git switch for branches, git restore for files. In the practicals we use switch.




Example of working on a branch
git switch -c new-plot
# ... edit files ...
git add .
git commit -m "Add PCA plot coloured by country"
git push -u origin new-plot
On the first push of a new branch, GitHub prints a link to open a Pull Request. This is a proposal to merge the branch into main, which collaborators can review.


Merging: git merge
Switch to the branch you want to update (usually main) and merge the other branch into it:
git switch main
git merge new-plot
git push

For the curious: working in a team
In larger projects with several collaborators, the team agrees on rules for branches. Simple rules that prevent a lot of trouble:

do not experiment directly on main,
always pull before you start working,
create a branch with a descriptive name for every new thing (new-plot, fix-readme),
merge the branch only when the code works,
write meaningful commit messages.

One of the best-known conventions is Git flow:



Git flow: main (stable version), develop (development), feature branches (new features), release (preparing a new version) and hotfix (urgent fixes).





Branch
Role




main
stable, released code


develop
ongoing development, integration of new features


feature/*
new features (from develop)


release/*
preparing a new version (from develop)


hotfix/*
urgent fixes (from main)




Merge or rebase?
Both commands bring work from one branch into another, but they treat history differently.
Merge keeps the actual history and creates an additional commit that joins the two branches:
A---B---C---F    (main, F = merge commit)
         \ /
          D---E  (branch)
Rebase “replants” your commits on top of the other branch, so the history is linear. The commit identifiers (hashes) change in the process:
A---B---C---D'---E'




Merge
Rebase




History
keeps branches
linear, cleaner


Safety on shared branches
safer
can confuse collaborators


Conflicts
resolved once
may appear for each commit



In the practicals we use merge. Rebase is useful once you are comfortable with the basics of collaboration.

section: Introduction to population genetics, genetic diversity and SNPs
text:
Introduction to population genetics, genetic diversity and SNPs
Population genetics is the study of genetic differences within and between populations. It focuses on understanding how these differences arise, how they are distributed, and their role in evolutionary processes. Key areas of research include adaptation, speciation and population structure.

Genetic diversity: the foundation of evolution
Genetic diversity refers to the variation in DNA sequences among individuals in a population. It plays a critical role in:

Adaptation: high genetic diversity increases the likelihood that some individuals in a population can survive and reproduce under changing environmental conditions.
Evolutionary potential: diversity provides the raw material for natural selection, enabling populations to evolve over time.

The DNA of any two humans is 99.6% identical, while the remaining 0.4% (approximately 12 million base pairs) accounts for individual differences. These variations can be neutral, beneficial or detrimental, depending on their context in the genome.


Single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs)
SNPs are the most common type of genetic variation and represent a change in a single nucleotide (A, C, T or G).

SNP: the minor allele is found in > 1% of the population.
Mutation: the minor allele is found in < 1% of the population.




A SNP and a mutation differ in the frequency of the minor allele in the population.



Key characteristics of SNPs

Frequency: SNPs account for 90% of human genetic variation.
Distribution: they occur approximately every 300 to 1000 base pairs in the genome.
Binarity: SNPs are typically biallelic, meaning there are two possible nucleotides at a given position.



Allele types at SNP loci

Major allele: the nucleotide found in more than 50% of the population.
Minor allele: the nucleotide found in less than 50% of the population. Its frequency is the MAF (minor allele frequency).

In VCF files we meet another naming: the reference allele (REF) is the one in the reference genome, the alternative allele (ALT) is the other one. The reference allele is not necessarily the major allele.
A diploid individual has one of three genotypes at each SNP:



Genotype
VCF code
Meaning




homozygous for the reference allele
0/0
e.g. A/A


heterozygous
0/1
A/G


homozygous for the alternative allele
1/1
G/G


missing genotype
./.
not enough reads at this position



Changes between two purines (A ↔︎ G) or two pyrimidines (C ↔︎ T) are transitions (Ts), all others are transversions (Tv). Transitions are more common in genomes, so the Ts/Tv ratio is a good indicator of variant calling quality (around 2–3 genome-wide in vertebrates).


SNPs in coding and non-coding regions
SNPs can occur in both non-coding and coding regions:

Non-coding regions: SNPs in these regions can affect gene regulation, splicing or the stability of RNA.
Coding regions: SNPs in these regions may be

synonymous: no change in the amino acid sequence due to redundancy in the genetic code,
nonsynonymous: a change in the amino acid sequence, potentially affecting the structure and function of the protein.





Types of single nucleotide changes.




SNPs as tools in research
Due to their abundance and ease of genotyping, SNPs have become the primary markers in association studies, which examine how genetic variations are linked to traits such as:

diseases: identifying genetic risk factors for conditions like diabetes or cancer,
phenotypes: understanding the genetic basis of traits like height, skin colour or metabolic differences.



The importance of studying SNPs
SNPs are invaluable for population genetics and genomics because they:

trace ancestry and population history: SNP patterns reveal migration, admixture and evolutionary history,
aid conservation biology: assess genetic diversity in endangered species to guide conservation efforts,
facilitate personalised medicine: help identify genetic variants associated with drug responses and diseases.

By exploring genetic diversity and SNPs, population genetics provides a powerful framework for understanding evolution, human health and biodiversity.

Bioinformatic pipeline to get SNPs
The diagram shows the pipeline to the final merged and filtered VCF file. After basic QC and the relatedness check the pipeline splits into a dataset without LD pruning and a dataset after LD pruning, because different analyses need different datasets.






Slika 6.1: From sample to SNP dataset. In this practical we start in column 3: basic QC and relatedness; then the path splits into a dataset without and with LD pruning.



From now on we will work in PLINK to do some analyses and prepare the data for R.






NasvetLinux



Large analyses are usually run on Linux servers (HPC), where PLINK is called directly from the terminal. PLINK also runs on Windows and macOS, so we will run it from R. The commands are the same. If you don’t know Linux, have a look at the basic Linux commands and the Linux chapter in Practical 0.



Biallelic variants in VCF files for PLINK
When preparing VCF (Variant Call Format) files for PLINK analysis, it’s crucial to understand and focus on biallelic variants.

What are biallelic variants?
Biallelic variants are genetic variations where only two alleles are observed at a specific locus (position) in a population. In the context of SNPs, this means there are only two possible nucleotides at a given position.


Why biallelic variants for PLINK?

Simplicity: PLINK is designed to work primarily with biallelic variants, as they are easier to analyse statistically (the PLINK 1 format cannot store others at all).
Common in SNPs: most SNPs are naturally biallelic, making them ideal for population genetics studies.
Computational efficiency: biallelic variants require fewer computational resources to process and analyse.



Preparing VCF files for PLINK

Filter for biallelic sites: remove any multiallelic variants (sites with more than two alleles) from your VCF file.
Check the REF and ALT columns: the REF column should contain one allele and the ALT column only one alternative allele.
Example: a valid biallelic entry looks like chr1 100 . A G . PASS ., where A is the reference and G the single alternative allele.



Important considerations

Quality control: make sure your variants pass appropriate quality filters before including them in your PLINK analysis.
Indels: while PLINK can handle biallelic insertions and deletions (indels), some analyses are more straightforward with SNPs only.
Documentation: always document any filtering steps you perform on your VCF file before the PLINK analysis.

By focusing on biallelic variants, you ensure compatibility with PLINK and set a solid foundation for your population genetics analyses.

PLINK from R
In the previous practicals we learned about R, RStudio and Quarto. R can run command-line programs with the system() function:

system("data/plink2.exe --version")

If plink2.exe is stored somewhere else than the data, we have to type the full path every time, which is not very clear:

text:
Data: white-tailed eagle
We use data from Hansen et al. (2023), Molecular Ecology: whole genomes (WGS) of 92 white-tailed eagles from Iceland (IS), Greenland (GL), Norway (NO), Denmark (DK), Estonia (ES) and one sample from Turkey (TU). Some samples are contemporary (Con, after 1990) and some historical (His, museum specimens from ~1880–1950).






OpozoriloWatch out: property of the data



The eagle VCF is already filtered and LD-pruned (r² > 0.5). The authors uploaded only the final dataset to Dryad, so:

we cannot repeat some filters (depth, genotype quality) from scratch, but we can check them,
the dataset contains only variable sites, and some linked SNPs have already been removed. This matters for π, SFS and ROH (Practicals 3 and 5).

Variants were called with GraphTyper2 on the golden eagle (Aquila chrysaetos) reference genome.



Folders and paths
Download E2_practical2_data.zip (100 MB) from GitHub and unzip it. You get the folder practical2 with this .qmd file, the images and the folder data. Add plink2.exe to the data folder and open E2_plink_EN.qmd in RStudio. The structure must be:
practical2/
├── E2_plink_EN.qmd
├── images/                   # figures
├── data/
│   ├── eagle.vcf.gz          # genotypes (VCF, compressed)
│   ├── eagle_metadata.csv    # one individual per line
│   ├── chromosoms_eagle.csv  # chromosome names
│   └── plink2.exe            # PLINK 2 (macOS/Linux: plink2)
└── results/                  # PLINK writes here (created automatically)
We set all paths once, at the beginning.

library(tidyverse)

data_dir    <- "data"      # folder with the data and PLINK 2
results_dir <- "results"   # PLINK writes its files here

The plink2() function
The function builds the command, prints it, runs it and shows the most important lines of the log (.log). It also adds --chr-set 26 no-x no-y no-xy no-mt, because the eagle has 26 autosomes. Without it, PLINK would treat chromosomes 23–26 as human X, Y, XY and MT.

plink2 <- function(..., show = TRUE) {
  args <- c(..., "--chr-set", "26", "no-x", "no-y", "no-xy", "no-mt", "--silent")
  out <- args[which(args == "--out") + 1]
  cat("plink2", c(...), "\n")

  # quotes around paths, so that folders with spaces also work
  windows <- .Platform$OS.type == "windows"
  command <- if (windows) plink2_path else shQuote(plink2_path)   # Windows adds quotes itself
  status <- system2(command, args = shQuote(args, type = if (windows) "cmd" else "sh"))

  log <- readLines(paste0(out, ".log"))
  if (status != 0) {
    cat(log, sep = "\n")
    stop("PLINK stopped with an error (see the log above).")
  }
  if (show) {
    cat(grep("loaded|remaining|removed|written|scanned", log, value = TRUE), sep = "\n")
  }
  invisible(log)
}

Relatedness and duplicated samples (KING)
Related individuals in a sample cause problems: they inflate allele frequencies of the family, and in structure analyses (PCA, ADMIXTURE) they can create false clusters. Duplicated samples (the same individual twice) are an error that we must remove.

KING-robust kinship estimator
Source: https://www.cog-genomics.org/plink/2.0/distance
The relationship matrix computed by --make-rel, --make-grm-list or --make-grm-bin can be used to reliably identify close relations within a single population, if your MAFs are decent. However, Manichaikul et al.’s KING-robust estimator (2010) can also be mostly trusted on mixed-population datasets, and doesn’t require MAFs at all. Therefore, PLINK 2 computes relatedness with KING.
The exception is that KING-robust underestimates kinship when the parents are from very different populations. PCA can help detect this.
Note that KING kinship coefficients are scaled such that duplicate samples have kinship 0.5, not 1. First-degree relations (parent-child, full siblings) correspond to ~0.25, second-degree relations to ~0.125, etc. It is conventional to use a cutoff of ~0.354 (the geometric mean of 0.5 and 0.25) to screen for monozygotic twins and duplicate samples, ~0.177 to add first-degree relations, etc.

Wahlund effect
If we pool several populations with different allele frequencies, we observe a deficit of heterozygotes, even if each population is in equilibrium. This is called the Wahlund effect. We test it by calculating HWE separately for two contemporary populations. The HWE test only makes sense for SNPs that are polymorphic in the group, so we exclude monomorphic ones.

Therefore we do not apply the HWE filter to pooled data. In practice it is applied within populations, removing only SNPs that deviate in several populations at once (which indicates a technical error, e.g. a paralog).



Filtering by chromosome
With --chr we keep only selected chromosomes. This is useful when we want to test an analysis on a smaller dataset first.

Be careful: for further filtering we use the whole dataset, not just chromosome 1.


Linkage disequilibrium (LD)
SNPs that lie close together are inherited together and carry similar information (linkage disequilibrium, LD). For PCA and ADMIXTURE, which assume independent SNPs, we therefore remove one SNP from each pair with high r² (LD pruning).
The command --indep-pairwise 50 5 0.2 scans windows of 50 SNPs, shifts the window by 5 SNPs and removes one SNP from each pair with r² > 0.2.

Our VCF is already pruned at r² 0.5. Additional pruning at r² 0.2 would remove many more SNPs, partly because r² is calculated over all populations together (population structure itself increases LD). Therefore we don’t apply it and keep the authors’ dataset. For analyses that need all SNPs (ROH, LD decay, π in windows), an unpruned dataset would be used in practice.

The diagram (Slika 6.1) splits after basic QC and relatedness into two datasets: without LD pruning and after LD pruning. Our data are only on the right branch. Before using them in Practicals 3–5, think about where this will affect the results.

These questions can help:

Does the method assume that SNPs are independent? What happens if the same information is counted several times?
Does the method look at individual SNPs or at runs of neighbouring SNPs (windows, segments)?
Does the estimate change, or only its confidence interval?

OpombaQuestion: F-statistics



Hansen et al. (2023) calculated FST on the pruned dataset. Would the global FST between Iceland and Norway change much if all SNPs were used? What about with --maf 0.05? Why does it matter for FIS and FH (plink --het) from which individuals the allele frequencies are calculated? (Hint: Wahlund effect in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (HWE).)





All in one command
All filters can be applied in a single command. PLINK applies them in a fixed order (individuals first, then SNPs), so we have to keep track ourselves of which filters were used:
./plink2.exe --bfile eagle_0 --geno 0.05 --mind 0.05 --maf 0.05 --hwe 1e-6 --indep-pairwise 50 5 0.2 --make-bed --out eagle_all
In this practical we filtered step by step, because this shows how many individuals and SNPs we lose with each filter (Filtering cascade and final dataset).






NasvetParameters from the literature



We don’t invent thresholds. We look them up in papers with similar data and cite them. The authors of the eagle paper used: QUAL ≥ 1000, GQ ≥ 20, DP ≥ 8, autosomes only, at most 25% missing genotypes per SNP, MQ ≥ 30, LD pruning r² 0.5 (window 134). Common PLINK QC values for animals are --geno 0.1–0.2, --mind 0.1–0.2 (much more lenient for ancient DNA), --maf 0.01–0.05, --hwe 1e-6 within populations. All chosen thresholds are reported in the methods.

Filtering cascade and final dataset
Finally we make a table: how many SNPs and individuals are left after each step. Such a table always goes into the methods or supplementary material.

count_files <- function(path) c(snp = length(readLines(paste0(path, ".bim"))),
                                ind = length(readLines(paste0(path, ".fam"))))

steps <- tribble(
  ~step,                                 ~command,                                ~file,
  "1 Biallelic SNPs (no indels)",        "`--snps-only just-acgt --max-alleles 2`", "eagle_0",
  "2 Individuals with ≤ 80% missing",    "`--mind 0.8`",                          "eagle_1_mind",
  "3 SNPs with ≤ 20% missing",           "`--geno 0.2`",                          "eagle_2_geno",
  "4 No duplicated samples",             "`--remove` (KING > 0.354)",             "eagle_3_no_duplicates",
  "5 MAF ≥ 0.05 (only for PCA, P4)",     "`--maf 0.05`",                          "eagle_4_maf05"
)

cascade <- steps |>
  mutate(n = map(file, \(f) count_files(r(f))),
         SNPs = map_int(n, "snp"),
         individuals = map_int(n, "ind")) |>
  select(-n)

bind_rows(tibble(step = "0 VCF (Dryad)", command = "", file = "eagle.vcf.gz",
                 SNPs = vcf_snp, individuals = length(columns) - 9L),
          cascade) |>
